In the mathematical discipline of [[measure theory]], the '''intensity''' of a [[Measure (mathematics)|measure]] is the average value the measure assigns to an interval of length one.

== Definition ==
Let <math> \mu </math> be a measure on the real numbers. Then the intensity <math> \overline \mu </math> of <math> \mu </math> is defined as

:<math> \overline \mu:= \lim_{|t| \to \infty} \frac{\mu((-s,t-s])}{t} </math>

if the limit exists and is independent of <math> s </math> for all <math> s \in \R </math>.

== Example ==
Look at the [[Lebesgue measure]] <math> \lambda </math>. Then for a fixed <math> s </math>, it is
:<math> \lambda((-s,t-s])=(t-s)-(-s)=t, </math>

so
:<math> \overline \lambda:= \lim_{|t| \to \infty} \frac{\lambda((-s,t-s])}{t}=  \lim_{|t| \to \infty} \frac t t =1. </math>

Therefore the Lebesgue measure has intensity one.

== Properties ==
The set of all measures <math> M </math> for which the intensity is well defined is a measurable subset of the set of all measures on <math> \R </math>. The mapping 
:<math> I \colon M \to \mathbb R </math>
defined by

:<math> I(\mu) = \overline \mu </math>

is [[Measurable function|measurable]].
